chapters.title: The first crossings
chapters.stat: Sea level 120 m lower at the glacial maximum
chapters.text:
People reached Sahul — Australia and New Guinea, then one landmass — around 65,000 years ago. Even at the lowest sea level of the last glacial cycle, that required crossing at least 70–90 km of open water, out of sight of land, with a target that could not be seen from the departure point.

No boat survives. The evidence is the arrival.
chapters.lede: Sea level 70 m lower. People cross 70–90 km of open water to a land they cannot see.
chapters.cite: Clarkson et al., *Nature* (2017); Kealy, Louys & O'Connor (2018); Spratt & Lisiecki sea-level stack (2016).

chapters.title: Reed, plank and the first sea trades
chapters.text:
The Bronze Age Mediterranean ran on sea-borne metal. The Uluburun wreck, about 1320 BC, was 15 m long and carried 354 oxhide copper ingots — ten tonnes — plus a tonne of tin, in exactly the ratio bronze needs.

Egypt was building 43 m hulls by 2566 BC. The Khufu ship has no keel and no frames: it is 1,224 pieces of cedar held with unpegged mortise-and-tenon joints and grass lashing, and it works.
chapters.lede: The Bronze Age Mediterranean runs on sea-borne metal, in hulls held together with mortise-and-tenon and grass.
chapters.cite: Bass & Pulak, Institute of Nautical Archaeology; Khufu ship, Grand Egyptian Museum.

chapters.title: The oared sea and the monsoon ocean
chapters.text:
Two oceans running on two different principles at the same time.

In the Mediterranean, oars — because a galley goes where it likes regardless of the wind, and the sea is small enough that it never has to go far. In the Indian Ocean, the monsoon, which reverses twice a year and fixes the sailing calendar of half the world.
chapters.lede: Two oceans on two principles at once: oars in the Mediterranean, and a wind that reverses twice a year in the Indian.
chapters.cite: Casson, *Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World*; *Periplus Maris Erythraei*.

chapters.title: Longships, junks and the sewn ocean
chapters.stat: Skuldelev 2: 30 m, 60 oars, built in Dublin in 1042
chapters.text:
The Norse reach North America; Chinese ships carry bulkheads, a sternpost rudder and a compass; the Indian Ocean is worked by sewn hulls with no iron in them at all; and Austronesian navigators have already settled the Pacific.

There is no single centre in this period, and any version of this story that puts one in Europe is wrong on the dates.
chapters.lede: No single centre. The Norse reach America, Chinese hulls carry bulkheads and a compass, and the Pacific is already settled.
chapters.cite: Viking Ship Museum Roskilde; Needham IV.3; Belitung wreck.

chapters.title: The ocean crossed, and taken
chapters.stat: 12.5 million people embarked on the Middle Passage
chapters.text:
In four centuries every ocean is crossed, charted and fought over. The instruments that made it possible — the *volta do mar*, the caravel, the carrack, latitude sailing, and eventually the chronometer — arrive alongside the uses they were put to.

The Atlantic's principal cargo in this period was human beings. That is not an aside from the technology; the ships were designed for it.
chapters.lede: Every ocean crossed, charted and fought over in four centuries — and the Atlantic’s principal cargo is people.
chapters.cite: Eltis & Richardson; Solar & de Zwart (2017); Portuguese *Regimento*.

chapters.title: Iron, steam, and the end of the wind
chapters.text:
Within a single lifetime the ocean stops being a wind field and becomes a distance. Iron hulls, screw propellers, and above all engines that burn a third as much coal for the same power.

The Suez Canal opens in 1869 and sail cannot use it. The fastest sailing ships ever built are launched in the same decade they are made obsolete.
chapters.lede: Within one lifetime the ocean stops being a wind field and becomes a distance.
chapters.cite: Griffiths, *Steam at Sea*; Suez Canal Authority.

chapters.title: Steel, and two wars at sea
chapters.stat: Battle of the Atlantic: ~14.7 M tons sunk by U-boats
chapters.text:
The dreadnought, the turbine, oil firing and the diesel motorship — and then two wars in which the decisive question is whether merchant ships can cross the Atlantic at all.

They could, from May 1943, when the mid-ocean air gap closed. Of about 40,000 men who served in U-boats, some 30,000 died: the highest loss rate of any arm of the German military.
chapters.lede: Two wars in which the question is whether merchant ships can cross the Atlantic at all.

chapters.title: The box, and the sea as a cost line
chapters.stat: ~24,000 TEU in one hull; ~80% of world trade by volume
chapters.text:
A steel box of standard dimensions, first carried on 26 April 1956, removes most of the cost of moving anything anywhere — and with it most of the reason for a port to be where it is.

The route of a modern ship is set by lock chambers and dredged channels rather than by wind. The ocean is still there; it has simply stopped being the thing that decides.
chapters.lede: A steel box of standard size removes most of the cost of moving anything anywhere — and most of the reason a port is where it is.
chapters.cite: Levinson, *The Box* (2006); UNCTAD Review of Maritime Transport.
